In summary, our research is concerned with
the way in which people evaluate food, and how these evaluations are constructed in conversation.
the way in which people use evaluative expressions in talk, and how these are related to the social activities in which the talk is embedded.
how people use evaluations to accomplish social actions in everyday life, and how this use is shaped by the social context in which it occurs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evaluative practices in this study are highly sensitive to the topic, and that they are not simply a reflection of underlying attitudes.
evaluations in everyday conversation are not a unitary phenomenon.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the evaluative practices in this study are not best understood as a reflection of underlying attitudes, but as part of a complex set of practices which include the evaluation of specific instances of food.
evaluative expressions are not simply the expression of attitudes, but are used to perform particular activities in specific social practices.
we are interested in how people talk about food and how this relates to their attitudes and practices.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of evaluative expressions is highly sensitive to the context in which they are used, and the way in which they are deployed is highly sensitive to their specific use in the interaction.
the use of the term 'attitude' is problematic, and that we should be cautious about treating all evaluative expressions as broadly equivalent.
evaluative practices are not a single phenomenon and should not be treated as such, as they are highly sensitive to the context in which they occur.
